title: Ephemeral Context Profiles — idea scratchpad
content:
Quick brain dump about a lightweight feature: Ephemeral Context Profiles (ECP).

Why: large apps keep stuffing conversation history into every request which inflates token cost and latency. We already have prefix/KV caching for transformer state, but teams still struggle to:
- surface only the signals that matter for a given route (e.g. shopping assistant vs billing assistant)
- let frontend decide a low-cost summary for long-lived sessions without server-side model switches
- experiment with context heuristics without changing model weights

Idea (one-liner): allow clients to attach short, named ephemeral "context profiles" that express which kinds of context should be materialized/expanded from the KV cache and which should be compressed/omitted. The runtime applies policy-driven trimming/expansion at serving time to keep tokens and latency under budget.

Core primitives (rough):
- Profile: small JSON-like structure (<= 1kB) with tags and rules, e.g. {name: 'purchase-flow', scopes: ['cart','payment'], compress: ['chitchat'], priority: 'high'}
- ProfileStore: ephemeral per-session store (TTL configurable) that the client can manage via API (create/update/delete/list).
- On-request header: x-ecp: purchase-flow or x-ecp: [inline profile blob] (for testing).
- Runtime policy layer: given profile + route/model profile + cached KV, produce a trimmed prompt/KV selection and optional summary token to prepend.

User stories (quick):
- As a frontend engineer, I want to attach a lightweight profile for the checkout route so that past browsing chatter is deprioritized and token budget goes to product state.
- As a product manager, I want to A/B two trimming strategies across a subset of users to measure impact on latency/cost and conversion.
- As an SRE, I want caps on profile store growth and eviction rules so a rogue client can't fill memory.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- API to create a profile and attach it to requests by name.
- Runtime honors profile by excluding at least one category (e.g., "chitchat") from prompt selection and reducing tokens by >= 10% on typical long sessions.
- Metrics surfaced: tokens/request, p95 latency, failed-trims (cases where profile conflicts with required context), profile-store size/evictions.

Design notes / constraints:
- Profile evaluation must be cheap (no model runs). Use metadata tags on cached entries (we already store "source" and "type" metadata in KV; extend with client-provided labels).
- Backwards compatibility: default behavior when no profile is present must be unchanged.
- Security: profiles are ephemeral and scoped to api-key/project. Prevent cross-tenant leakage.
- UI: Redwood Console can show active profiles, approximate savings, and let you run a dry-run to see what would be dropped.

Runtime approach ideas (tradeoffs):
1) Heuristic tag filter (fast): store tags on each cached chunk (e.g., user-message:chat, system:instructions, cart:state). Evaluate profile as allowlist/denylist. Pros: cheap, predictable. Cons: semantic tagging must be accurate.
2) Lightweight compression scoring (medium): score cached chunks with a small, cached embedding and evict lowest-relevance by profile weighting. Pros: adaptable. Cons: needs embedding compute and extra storage.
3) Model-based summary (heavy): when profile demands aggressive trimming, run a short summary generation to condense old context. Pros: best quality. Cons: cost and latency.

MVP should start with (1) + hooks to enable (2) later.

Metrics to track:
- tokens_saved_per_request (rolling 7d)
- p95 and p50 latency change (profile vs baseline)
- model-accuracy/regression metrics on eval prompt sets (we must ensure trimming doesn't regress quality)
- profile_create_rate, profile_eviction_rate, active_profile_per_key

Experiment plan (6 weeks):
Week 0: implement profile store + header passthrough + tag-based filters in runtime (no UI). Add logging and metric tags.
Week 1-2: internal dogfood on a couple small Redwood apps (solutions-engineering + demo customers) using inline profiles. Collect metrics.
Week 3: add dry-run mode (simulate trim but keep full prompt) and a simple console debug view.
Week 4: rollout A/B test to 10% of hosted API keys with low-risk routes. Measure quality/regression for 2 weeks.
Week 6: decide on staged rollout or iterate on scoring approach.

Open questions / parking-lot:
- How to tag KV entries reliably? Instrument frontend SDK to attach tags on writes? Or run an automated classifier during caching? (tradeoff: client integration friction vs server CPU)
- TTL: default ephemeral profile TTL (1h? 24h?) and max total profiles per key.
- Offline tooling to preview "what would be trimmed" using stored session replays. Would help product/eval teams.
- UX for composing profiles (inheritance, channel-specific overrides).
- Interaction with rollouts: if a profile triggers a summary (model call), should we count it against customer quota or Redwood's internal budget?

Implementation notes (todo):
- [ ] proto API + swagger (simple POST /projects/:id/profiles)
- [ ] runtime rule engine: very small policy eval library (Go) to run in the fast path
- [ ] metric tags + logging: token savings per request, reason codes
- [ ] storage: redis with LRU + small metadata store for tags and creation time
- [ ] console: table view + dry-run output (text diff of trimmed segments)
- [ ] integration test: replay test sessions to ensure no regression on 10 eval prompts

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: trimming too aggressively leads to hallucinations/regressions. Mitigate: default to conservative denylist and require dry-run / A/B before full enable.
- Risk: client tags are noisy/misleading. Mitigate: provide client SDK helpers (type-safe tag enums) and server-side heuristics fallback.
- Risk: storage blowup from many profiles. Mitigate: quota, TTL, and periodic compaction.

Notes to self: ping @evan-park about embedding-backed scoring experiment and ask @maya-singh for a small eval set (checkout flow + billing Qs). Put a sprint ticket if PM likes the idea.

End of scratchpad. This is intentionally rough — next step is to convert into compact PRD with acceptance criteria and risk matrix if stakeholders want to pursue.
